series: HTTPS & TLS: THE HANDSHAKE HANDBOOK — PART 2

items: TLS False Start sent data right after Finished
A TLS 1.2-era trick, superseded by 1.3's 1-RTT
Connection reuse is the bigger lever anyway
Keep-alive and HTTP/2 amortize one handshake over hundreds
OCSP stapling saves an RTT and a lookup to the CA

blocks.title: Tickets Track You
items: A ticket is a unique identifier you hand back
Servers can correlate it across visits
Which is why browsers scope and expire per-site
Destination IP and port — routing demands it
The DNS query for the hostname, unless DoH or DoT
SNI in ClientHello, unless ECH is on both ends
The whole server cert in TLS 1.2, but not in 1.3
ALPN, naming HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3

left.title: Leaked
items: IP + port
DNS name
SNI
sizes + timing

right.title: Encrypted
items: URL path + query
HTTP headers
cookies
request + response bodies
Packet sizes, timing and direction stay visible
That alone names which page of a site you loaded
Which video you streamed, which app you are running
Total bytes and duration fingerprint odd workloads

blocks.title: JA3 / JA4
items: Fingerprint from cipher and extension ordering
Derived straight from your ClientHello
Identifies your TLS stack, often the exact app or bot
Tokens in a query string land in server logs
And browser history, `Referer`, analytics pipelines
TLS protects the wire and nothing past it
The server decrypts everything on arrival
What happens next is not TLS's problem
Enterprise installs its own root on managed devices
The proxy decrypts and re-encrypts every flow
Traffic fully visible, padlock still showing
Captive portals do the same via an installed profile

blocks.title: Padlock Is Not Privacy
blocks.text: On a managed device the lock tells you the connection is encrypted to the proxy — and says nothing about who reads it after that.
TLS hides WHAT you said. It does not hide WHO you talked to, WHEN, HOW MUCH, or HOW OFTEN.

blocks.q: Can an observer tell which video I watched?
a_bullets: Yes — from segment sizes and their timing
TLS pads and delays nothing by default
Cover traffic is the only real defence

items: CRIME / BREACH: compression plus secrets is an oracle
FREAK / Logjam (2015): export-grade downgrade
ROBOT (2017): the RSA padding oracle, again
Heartbleed leaked private keys straight out of memory
Common thread: a legacy feature or a downgrade path

blocks.title: Delete, Do Not Patch
blocks.text: TLS 1.3 removed the features these attacks used instead of hardening them. Removed code has no oracle.

slides.page_title: Failures, Fixes, and the Field Checklist

items: A wrong client clock looks exactly like expiry
Stale CA bundles also cause local-issuer errors
Fix the chain — never disable verification
Add the proxy root deliberately, not blindly
TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only, nothing older
ECDHE-only key exchange, AEAD ciphers only
Disable renegotiation and compression
Enable OCSP stapling
Serve leaf plus intermediates, never the root
Prefer ECDSA with an RSA fallback for old clients
HSTS `max-age` of a year plus `includeSubDomains`
Add `preload` only once every subdomain is HTTPS
Rotate session ticket keys on a schedule

slides.page_title: Failures, Fixes, and the Field Checklist (cont.)

items: ACME clients: certbot, lego, caddy, cert-manager
With 47-day certs, manual renewal is planned downtime
Alert on expiry at 14 days, not at 1
Monitor CT logs for certs you never requested

blocks.title: Key Hygiene
items: Keep private keys out of disk backups
A leaked key is a full-site compromise
Revoke, reissue, then rotate everything downstream

blocks.text: TLS wraps TCP to give confidentiality, integrity and server authentication; certificates chain a hostname to a trusted root.

blocks.title: One Line
blocks.text: SNI tells the server which cert to send and leaks the hostname doing it; resumption trades a little forward secrecy for a lot of latency; and the tunnel hides your content while broadcasting your metadata.

caption.text: Part 2 of HTTPS & TLS: THE HANDSHAKE HANDBOOK. The padlock does not mean the site is safe — it means the bytes are encrypted to whoever answered the phone. This handbook walks the TLS 1.2 and 1.3 handshakes packet by packet, decodes certificate chains and SAN matching, explains why SNI still leaks every hostname you visit, and ends with the config checklist and error-triage table you actually reach for at 2am. 10 pages, no fluff: internals, trade-offs, and the misconfigurations that bite in production.
